The  '''McCook Detention Center''', nicknamed the ''''Cornhusker Clink'''',<ref>{{Cite news |last=Bailey |first=Ruth |date=June 16, 2026 |title=‘McCook's ‘Cornhusker Clink’ divides community, sparks financial questions |url=https://nebraskapublicmedia.org/en/news/news-articles/mccooks-cornhusker-clink-divides-community-sparks-financial-questions/ |work=[[Nebraska Public Media]]}}</ref> is an [[Immigration detention in the United States|immigration detention center]] in [[McCook, Nebraska]], United States. The center was announced in August 2025 and officially opened in November. It was developed by the [[United States Department of Homeland Security|Department of Homeland Security]] and is operated by the [[Nebraska Department of Correctional Services]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Timotija |first=Filip |date=August 19, 2025 |title=‘Cornhusker Clink’: DHS to open new ICE migrant detention facility in Nebraska |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/5460723-cornhusker-clink-dhs-to-open-new-ice-migrant-detention-facility-in-nebraska/ |work=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]}}</ref> The plan for the facility was to convert the McCook Work Ethic Camp, a rehabilitative minimum-security prison labor camp, to a detention center for the [[United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement]] (ICE) with an expansion to 280 beds. Development came after other immigration detention centers, like [[Alligator Alcatraz]] in Florida, were opened by the [[Second presidency of Donald Trump|Trump Administration]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Tedesco |first=Maria |date=2025-08-19 |title='Cornhusker Clink,' Trump admin to open new migrant detention center in Nebraska |url=https://13wham.com/news/nation-world/cornhusker-clink-trump-admin-to-open-new-migrant-detention-center-nebraska-alligator-alcatraz-deportation-depot-coyote-compound-lonestar-lockup-aclu-trump-administration-tom-homan |access-date=2025-08-20 |website=[[WHAM-TV]] |language=en}}</ref>

== History ==
The McCook Work Ethic Camp was originally authorized in 1997 and opened in 2001.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=November 1, 2023 |title=WORK ETHIC CAMP LEGISLATIVE REPORT |url=https://nebraskalegislature.gov/FloorDocs/108/PDF/Agencies/Correctional_Services__Department_of/239_20231229-082800.pdf |website=Nebraska Department of Correctional Services}}</ref> Its aim was to [[Rehabilitation (penology)|rehabilitate]] prisoners before they left prison to enter wider society. Most prisoners were transferred to the Work Ethic Camp from other prisons in Nebraska near the ends of their sentences.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bailey |first=Ruth |date=2026-06-16 |title=Nebraska’s ‘Cornhusker Clink’ divides community, sparks financial questions |url=https://www.kcur.org/news/2026-06-16/nebraskas-cornhusker-clink-divides-community-sparks-financial-questions |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=KCUR - Kansas City news and NPR |language=en}}</ref>

A plan to transform the camp to an ICE detention facility was made with a three-year agreement between Nebraska governor [[Jim Pillen]] and the DHS with [[Kristi Noem]] on August 19, 2025.<ref name="APNews">{{Cite web |last=Funk |first=Josh |date=2025-08-19 |title=Nebraska announces plan for immigration detention center dubbed the 'Cornhusker Clink' |url=https://apnews.com/article/nebraska-ice-detention-center-immigration-1ae76a48f62a7304da63e2780a357190 |access-date=2025-08-20 |website=[[AP News]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=McCann |first=Allison |date=December 7, 2025 |title=This Prison Rehabilitated Inmates. Until ICE Paid to Fill It With Immigrants |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/07/world/nebraska-prison-mccook-ice-immigrants-detention-trump.html |work=The New York Times}}</ref> The agreement included an expansion to house 300 inmates, up from 200 as of 2023, up to 365 days.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" /> Pillen stated that he did not know if the prison would house women and children in addition to men. He also announced that the [[Nebraska National Guard]] would be ordered to provide logistical and administrative support to ICE agents based in Nebraska. To make room for the detention center, all 186 inmates that were at the Work Ethic Camp were moved to different facilities.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last= |first= |last2= |first2= |last3= |first3= |date=2025-08-20 |title=Nebraska announces plan for immigration detention center dubbed the ‘Cornhusker Clink’ |url=https://www.wymt.com/2025/08/20/nebraska-announces-plan-immigration-detention-center-dubbed-cornhusker-clink/ |access-date=2025-08-20 |website=WYMT |language=en}}</ref>

Several lawsuits were filed in order to prevent the detention center's opening. Most notably, The attempt to create an injunction to block the opening of the facility was itself blocked by Judge Patrick Heng. The lawsuit delayed the opening of the facility, and Heng allowed for the facility to open in early November.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Attridge |first=Margaret |date=2025-10-27 |title=Judge lets ICE turn Nebraska prison into 'Cornhusker Clink' |url=https://www.courthousenews.com/judge-lets-ice-turn-nebraska-prison-into-cornhusker-clink |access-date=2025-11-05 |website=Courthouse News Service |language=en-us}}</ref> On November 3, Pillen stated that it was expected to become operational by the end of that week.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dvorak |first=Gina |date=2025-11-03 |title=Pillen says ICE inmates expected at McCook facility this week |url=https://www.wowt.com/2025/11/03/pillen-says-ice-inmates-expected-mccook-facility-this-week/ |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=WOWT |language=en}}</ref> Three days later, Cornhusker Clink officially began operations.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Beck |first=-Margery A. |last2=Beck |first2=Associated Press Margery A. |last3=Press |first3=Associated |date=2025-11-06 |title=Nebraska converts prison into federal immigration center, aims to fill it by Thanksgiving |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/nebraska-converts-prison-into-federal-immigration-center-aims-to-fill-it-by-thanksgiving |access-date=2025-11-14 |website=PBS News |language=en-us}}</ref>

== Reactions ==
Upon its announcement, the prison received criticism from many Nebraska lawmakers and the Nebraska [[ACLU]].<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2025-08-19 |title=‘Cornhusker Clink’: Nebraska politicians, organizations react to Pillen announcement |url=https://www.wowt.com/2025/08/19/cornhusker-clink-nebraska-politicians-organizations-react-pillen-announcement/ |access-date=2025-08-20 |website=[[WOWT]] |language=en}}</ref> Protestors sat outside of the governor's office on the afternoon after the announcement.<ref name="APNews" /> Pillen and the DHS also received criticism for using the word "[[Nebraska Cornhuskers|Cornhusker]]" in the detention center's name, which is a moniker used by the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]] for their sports teams. The [[University of Nebraska system]] issued a statement distancing themselves from the Cornhusker Clink, and that they did not give permission for the moniker to be used.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dunker |first=Chris |date=2025-08-20 |title=University of Nebraska distances itself from 'Cornhusker Clink' detention center name |url=https://journalstar.com/news/state-regional/government-politics/article_c54adc00-0a9d-4528-bbfe-07aef6c391e0.html |access-date=2025-08-21 |website=JournalStar.com |language=en}}</ref> While the term "Cornhusker" is officially trademarked by the University of Nebraska system, they also recognize it as a common word and did not prevent the state from using it for the prison.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Monroe |first=Waverle |date=2025-08-20 |title=Cornhusker copyright? Getting the facts for the name of Nebraska's new ICE detention facility |url=https://www.ketv.com/article/nebraska-cornhusker-clink-copyright-ice-detention-facility/65840208 |access-date=2025-08-21 |website=KETV |language=en}}</ref>
